title: Clean Water, Fewer Diseases
goal: Learn the problem/solution text structure and its signal words; learn clarifying/inference as a comprehension strategy; practice pronoun reference tracing on a real sentence from today's text; close Unit A (Body & Health) with a short synthesis task comparing two Unit A texts.

prompts: "What signal words tell us a text is using cause/effect structure?" (because, as a result, therefore, due to, so, consequently, leads to)
"What does 'monitoring/fix-up' mean when you're reading?" (noticing when you've lost understanding, and having a plan to fix it — reread, read on, or check a word's parts)
"Name one organ or system we've learned about so far in Unit A." (any answer from L6.01–L6.03)

vocab.def: systems and practices — like clean toilets, sewers, and waste disposal — that keep water and surroundings free from germs and dirt.
examples: Good sanitation, like proper sewer systems, keeps human waste from contaminating drinking water.
The town improved its sanitation by building a modern water treatment plant.
vocab.task: "Name one example of good sanitation and one example of poor sanitation, and explain the difference between them."

vocab.def: to make something dirty, polluted, or unsafe by adding something harmful to it.
examples: Sewage leaking into a river can contaminate the drinking water downstream.
Unwashed hands can contaminate food before it's eaten.
vocab.task: "Which is more likely to contaminate a water supply, a well far from any sewage, or a well right next to an open drain? Explain your reasoning."

fluency.title: Read it smoothly
paragraphs: "When a community builds a water treatment system, it removes harmful bacteria and parasites before they ever reach a household tap, which means fewer people fall ill and fewer children miss school because of it."

facts: Water can carry disease-causing germs if it isn't treated or is allowed near waste.
Simple, low-cost fixes — boiling water, purification tablets, proper toilets — can break the cycle from contamination to illness.
Clean water and good sanitation work together; neither one alone fully solves the problem.
prime.question: Does your family boil drinking water, use a filter, or trust the tap directly? Why do you think that choice matters?
prime.intro: Before reading, briefly build the picture: "Picture the water pump or tap your own family uses at home, or a water tanker delivering to your street — now imagine tracing that water all the way back to where it came from, and asking what might have gotten into it along the way."

write.task: In 4–6 sentences, compare L6.03 (Why We Get Sick) and L6.04 (Clean Water, Fewer Diseases). Both texts are about disease, but one focuses on how the body reacts to germs already inside it, and the other focuses on stopping germs from getting in in the first place. Explain this difference in your own words, and name one signal word or phrase from each text that helped you notice its structure.
write.model: L6.03 explains what happens after a germ has already entered the body — it uses cause/effect signal words like 'because' and 'as a result' to show how the immune system reacts and causes symptoms like fever. L6.04 explains how to stop germs from reaching the body in the first place, through clean water and sanitation — it uses problem/solution language like 'the problem' and 'one answer' to lay out the challenge and its fixes. Together, the two texts show two different lines of defense against disease: the body's internal response, and public health prevention outside the body. Both agree that germs are the underlying cause of illness, just at different points in the story.

items.q: What two types of germs does the text say contaminated water can carry?
items.a: Bacteria (that cause cholera and typhoid) and parasites.

items.q: Name the two main solutions the text describes for the clean water problem.
items.a: Water treatment (filtration, chlorination, boiling, purification tablets) and sanitation infrastructure (toilets, sewage systems, paired with hygiene education).

items.q: Why does the text pair water treatment with sanitation improvements, rather than presenting only one as "the" solution?
items.a: Because contamination can happen at more than one point — in the water source itself, or later through unsafe handling — so both solutions are needed to fully break the cycle.

items.q: What does the phrase "even clean water can become contaminated again" imply about handwashing's role in this problem?
items.a: It implies that treating water once isn't enough on its own; unwashed hands or unsafe storage can reintroduce germs afterward, so handwashing is a necessary complement to clean water, not a separate issue.

items.q: The text says clean water access is "one of the oldest and most solvable problems in public health," yet still unsolved for millions. Do you find that framing convincing, or does it feel contradictory? Explain your view.
items.a: Either view is acceptable if justified — e.g., "convincing, because it distinguishes between the problem being technically solvable and it actually being solved everywhere due to resources/infrastructure gaps" or "it feels a little contradictory at first, since 'most solvable' sits oddly next to 'millions still lack access,' though the text does explain this is about implementation, not scientific difficulty."

check.support: If the learner scores below 4/5, reread the water treatment and sanitation paragraphs together, having them point to the sentence that names each of the two solutions before retrying questions 3 and 4.
check.challenge: If the learner scores 5/5 well under time, ask them to propose a third possible solution to the clean-water problem (not named in the text) and justify which of the two named solutions it's closer to.

passages.title: Clean Water, Fewer Diseases
paragraphs: Access to clean water is one of the oldest problems in public health. It's also one of the most solvable. Yet it remains a serious challenge in many parts of the world. The problem is straightforward to state: contaminated water can carry disease-causing germs. Human or animal waste can get into the water. That water may then carry bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid, or parasites that cause other serious illnesses. Those germs go directly into the mouths of anyone who drinks the water, cooks with it, or washes food in it.

Contamination usually happens when sanitation is poor. Sewage or waste from toilets, farms, or open drains sometimes isn't properly contained. It can then seep into rivers, wells, and underground water sources. Communities rely on those same sources for drinking water. In places without safe sanitation, this creates a repeating cycle. Contaminated water causes illness. Illness — especially diarrheal disease in young children — can itself cause dehydration, malnutrition, and even death, if left untreated.

One answer to this problem is water treatment, well established in public health research. When a community builds a water treatment system, it removes harmful bacteria and parasites. This happens before those germs ever reach a household tap. As a result, fewer people fall ill, and fewer children miss school because of it. Treatment methods range widely. In cities, this often means large-scale filtration and chlorination plants. In places without full infrastructure, simple household solutions work too — boiling water, or using approved water-purification tablets.

A second solution addresses the sanitation side of the problem directly. It means building proper toilets and sewage systems, so waste never reaches the water supply in the first place. This is often paired with basic hygiene education. Even clean water can become contaminated again, if it's stored, handled, or poured with unwashed hands. Public health research has repeatedly linked improved sanitation and handwashing habits to real drops in diarrheal disease and other water-related illness.

In response to this well-understood problem, governments, international organizations, and local communities have spent decades building wells, treatment plants, and sanitation systems. Their shared goal is breaking the contamination-to-illness cycle. Progress has been real and measurable in many regions. Still, the challenge is far from fully solved worldwide — millions of people still lack reliable access to safely managed drinking water. That's why clean water and sanitation remain a central, ongoing global health priority. Remember from L6.02 how blood carries oxygen through the body in a continuous loop? Clean water works on a similar idea, at a community scale. Instead of a pump moving oxygen through blood vessels, a treatment system moves safe water through pipes. Either loop breaking down causes serious harm downstream.

questions.q: What two kinds of germs can contaminated water carry, according to the text?
questions.a: Bacteria (which can cause cholera and typhoid) and parasites (which cause other serious illnesses).

questions.q: Why does the text call this a "repeating cycle"?
questions.a: Because contaminated water causes illness, and that illness — especially in young children — can itself lead to further harm, so poor sanitation and illness keep reinforcing each other unless something breaks the cycle.

questions.q: What does the text say basic hygiene education is often paired with?
questions.a: Building proper toilets and sewage systems (the sanitation solution) — because even clean water can be recontaminated by unwashed hands.

roles.prompt: Before you read a paragraph, glance at its first sentence. Say what you think it will tell you, in one sentence.
After you read a paragraph, ask one real question about it, not a question you already know the answer to. A good question usually starts with why, how, or what would happen if.
Find one word or one sentence in the paragraph that felt confusing or unclear. Say what confused you, then work out what it means using the words around it.
Say the paragraph's main point in one sentence, in your own words.
